description: Hands in a diamond, count your clean reps. Your diamond push-up number reveals the triceps tendon, the cable behind every lockout. Learn how this tendon transfers pressing power, the five mistakes that waste it, and the slow pressing protocol that builds it.

scenes.narration: Hands under your chest. | Thumbs and fingers touching. | That is the diamond. | Body in one line. | Now do push-ups. | Clean reps only. | Chest to your hands. | All the way up. | Elbows track back, | not out wide. | Count every good rep | until your form breaks. | Shaking is fine. | Collapsing is the end. | Your arms will burn. | That burn is not | the thing being tested. | Got your NUMBER? | Write it down. | At the end | I will tell you | what it says | about the cable | behind your elbow, | the triceps tendon.

scenes.label: CLEAN DIAMOND PUSH-UPS
scenes.narration: Here is the line. TWENTY clean diamond push-ups means your triceps tendon is transferring force from muscle to bone without leaking. Under eight is where most guys land, because the diamond removes every helper and bills the triceps alone. Over twenty-five, your lockout is a weapon, and lockouts are what finish presses, dips, and handstands. This number is a tendon report, not a chest report.
scenes.sub: under 8: leaking cable - 8 to 19: building - over 25: wired lockout

scenes.narration: Feel the back of your elbow, that bony point. Anchored right there is the TRICEPS TENDON, the single cable through which the entire triceps muscle pulls. The triceps is a big muscle with three heads, but all three heads funnel into this one tendon, and the tendon alone turns contraction into a straightening arm. That funnel is why the diamond push-up is so revealing. The narrow hand position shifts the work onto the triceps and its tendon, especially in the last part of the press, the LOCKOUT, where the elbow straightens against the most resistance. A soft tendon stretches and absorbs force that should have moved you. A stiff, trained tendon transfers it instantly. When guys say their pressing feels strong at the bottom and dead at the top, they are usually describing a cable problem wearing a muscle costume. The funnel shape explains one more thing: why the triceps tendon prefers honest tempo. When three heads contract together, force converges fast, and a jerky rep spikes the load at the anchor before the tissue can organize. A smooth rep lets the collagen fibers line up and share the pull. Same weight, same muscle, completely different experience for the cable. Tempo is not style. For a funnel tendon, tempo is safety and signal at the same time.

The science of this tendon follows the same law as every cable on this channel, with one twist. Tendons remodel in response to sustained tension, and they remodel most where the tension is highest. For the triceps tendon, that means two neighborhoods: the deep stretch at the bottom of the press, and the hard squeeze at the very top. Training that rushes through both, bouncing the middle, gives the tendon the least signal exactly where it needs the most. This is why pausing works so well here. A two-second pause at the bottom loads the tendon in its stretch. A two-second squeeze at the top loads it in its lock. Slow down both ends and the same set of push-ups becomes a tendon session instead of a muscle pump with the cables just along for the ride. This is also why lockout squeezes feel so different from mid-range reps. At full extension the tendon is the shortest, stiffest version of itself, and holding there teaches it to be a bar instead of a band.

beats.text: DIPS RUN ON THIS CABLE TOO
FIX THE CABLE, FIX THE PRESS

scenes.narration: Now notice how far this one cable reaches. Dips run on it. Close-grip presses run on it. The top of every regular push-up runs on it, and one day, your handstand push-up will live or die on it. The triceps tendon is the shared exit door for all pressing power, which makes it one of the highest-leverage tendons a skinny guy can train. There is also a warning built into its anatomy. Because all three heads funnel into one anchor, overload shows up in one place: a sore, stiff point right behind the elbow. That soreness is the tendon asking for the load to be managed, not ignored and not feared. Managed load, applied patiently, is exactly how it answers by getting stronger.

beats.text: YOUR WEIGHT IS THE RIGHT WEIGHT

scenes.narration: Your advantage is the same beautiful math as always. A diamond push-up charges you your own bodyweight, and your bodyweight is modest. The heavy guy's set ends at rep eight because his muscles are flooded, long before his tendon collects a real dose. You can live in the teens and twenties, stacking clean, full-tension reps, each one a deposit in the cable. Tendons do not ask how much the rep weighed. They ask how much clean tension arrived, and how often. Light guys deliver more of both. That is why the skinny guy who trains diamonds patiently ends up with the lockout that surprises everyone in the gym. The diamond also forgives small spaces. A square meter of floor is a complete triceps gym when the cable is the target.
Press with me. Diamond push-ups, thirty seconds of work, thirty of rest, four rounds. Pause one second at the bottom, squeeze one second at the top. Clean beats fast. Go.

Now the five mistakes destroying your triceps tendon. Mistake one: HALF REPS. Skipping the bottom skips the stretch load, skipping the top skips the lockout, and the tendon only gets the easy middle. Mistake two: elbows flared wide, which turns the diamond back into a chest exercise and unloads the cable you came to train. Mistake three: never pausing, so tension never sits anywhere long enough to send the building signal. Mistake four: testing your max every session, turning training into weekly exams the tendon cannot recover from. Mistake five: ignoring that sore point behind the elbow until a managed ache becomes a stubborn one. The fix is written into the test itself: full range, elbows tracking back, pauses at both ends, and max tests saved for retest day. And if that spot behind your elbow stays sore for weeks despite sensible loading, get it checked by a professional. Tendons respect honesty. Keep a simple log: date, clean reps, and how the lockout felt. Tendon progress hides inside how reps feel weeks before it shows in the count, and the log catches what memory misses.

scenes.label: RETEST THE DIAMOND
scenes.narration: So, your number. Under EIGHT: the cable is leaking, which is normal, common, and fixable. Eight to nineteen: the transfer is improving, and paused reps will push you quickly. Over TWENTY: your triceps tendon delivers what the muscle promises, and that is rarer than a big chest. Same rules in thirty days: chest to hands, full lockout, form break ends it. Put today's number in the comments. Just the number. In a month, that thread will show exactly who trained the cable and who just trained the pump.
scenes.sub: chest to hands, full lockout, form break ends it

scenes.narration: Your lockout was never about effort. It was about one cable behind your elbow. Give it thirty days of honest tension and bring me the new number. Subscribe, because next we test the smallest cables in the pressing chain: your wrists. This is {channel}. Train the cable.

title: 5 triceps tendon training Mistakes That Are Destroying Your triceps tendon
